'''''Solanum elaeagnifolium''''', the '''silverleaf nightshade'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SOEL|taxon=Solanum elaeagnifolium|accessdate=17 November 2015}}</ref> or '''silver-leaved nightshade''',  is a species of plant in the [[Solanaceae|nightshade family]] native to North and South America. It is common in parts of southwestern USA, and sometimes [[weed]] of western North America. Other common names include '''prairie berry''', '''silverleaf nettle''', '''white horsenettle''' or '''silver nightshade'''. In [[South Africa]] it is known as '''silver-leaf bitter-apple''' or '''''satansbos''''' ("[[Satan]]'s bush" in [[Afrikaans]]). More ambiguous names include '''"[[bull-nettle]]"''', '''"[[horsenettle]]"''' and the [[Spanish language|Spanish]] '''''"[[trompillo]]"'''''.<ref>Cronquist ''et al.'' (1984), USDA (2006)</ref>

''Solanum elaeagnifolium'' was described by [[Antonio José Cavanilles|A. J. Cavanilles]]. The plant described under the same name by [[William Herbert (botanist)|W. Herbert]] and [[Carl Byrd (Botanist)|C. L. Willdenow]] based on [[Ernst Gottlieb von Steudel|E.G. von Steudel]] is ''[[Solanum aethiopicum]]''.

==Description==
[[File:Androceo y gineceo de Solanum elaeagnifolium.jpg|thumb|left|Closeup of ''S. elaeagnifolium'' flower]]
[[File:Solanum elaeagnifolium berries.jpg|thumb|left|Closeup of ''S. elaeagnifolium'' berries]]
It is a [[perennial plant|perennial]] {{cvt|10|cm}}<ref>Niehaus ''et al.'' (1984)</ref> to 1 m in height. The stems are covered with nettle-like [[spine (botany)|spine]]s less than {{cvt|0.5|cm}} long,<ref name=npd>{{cite web |url=https://agri.nv.gov/Plant/Noxious_Weeds/WeedList/Silverleaf_nightshade_(Solanum_elaegnifolium)/ |title=''Solanum elaeagnifolium'' Cav. |work=Noxious weeds |publisher=Nevada Department of Agriculture |date=July 25, 2021 |accessdate=July 25, 2023 }}</ref> ranging from very few on some plants to very dense on others.  Leaves and stems are covered with downy hairs ([[trichome]]s) that lie against and hide the surface, giving a silvery or grayish appearance.<ref name = cronquistetal1984>Cronquist ''et al.'' (1984)</ref>

The leaves are up to 15 cm long and 0.5 to 2.5 cm wide, with shallowly waved edges, which distinguish it from the closely related [[Carolina Horsenettle]] (''S. carolinense''), which has wider, more deeply indented leaves.  The flowers, appearing from April to August, have five petals united to form a star, ranging from blue to pale lavender or occasionally white; five yellow [[stamen]]s and a [[pistil]] form a projecting center.  The plant produces glossy yellow, orange, or red [[berry (botany)|berries]] that last all winter and may turn brown as they dry.<ref name = cronquistetal1984 />

==Ecology==
It can grow in poor soil with very little water. It spreads by [[rhizome]]s as well as seeds, and is common in disturbed habitats. It is very hard to control, as root stocks less than 1 cm long can regenerate into plants.<ref>CDFA [2008]</ref>

Its distribution around the globe is in the regions of Mediterranean, South Australia, South Africa, US, Mexico and South America.<ref>{{cite web|title=Recorded occurrence of ''Solanum elaeagnifolium'' |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/cms/asset/5aaee890-fa62-4a88-af67-1e221facebd1/wre12556-fig-0001-m.jpg}}</ref> In the US, its range is from [[Kansas]] south to [[Louisiana]], and west through the Mexican-border states of the [[United States]] into and in [[Mexico]]. In South America it is found in [[Uruguay]], [[Argentina]], and [[Chile]].<ref name = usda2006>USDA (2006)</ref> It may have originated in North America and been accidentally introduced to South America<ref name = wsnwcb2008>WSNWCB (2008)</ref> or the reverse.<ref name = usda2006 /> It is considered a [[noxious weed]] in 21 U.S. states and in countries such as [[Australia]], [[Egypt]], [[Greece]], [[India]], [[Israel]], [[Italy]], [[South Africa]], and [[Zimbabwe]].<ref>Nugent (2005), WSNWCB (2008)</ref>

In a 15-year research study<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.3390/plants10040805 | doi-access=free | title=Investigating the Invasion Pattern of the Alien Plant Solanum elaeagnifolium Cav. (Silverleaf Nightshade): Environmental and Human-Induced Drivers | date=2021 | last1=Krigas | first1=Nikos | last2=Tsiafouli | first2=Maria A. | last3=Katsoulis | first3=Georgios | last4=Votsi | first4=Nefta-Eleftheria | last5=Van Kleunen | first5=Mark | journal=Plants | volume=10 | issue=4 | page=805 | pmid=33923898 | pmc=8072529 }}</ref> it was indicated that important factors for its expansion are:
Elevation of 0-100m,  soils with fine texture and in [[subsoil]] of medium water availability,  soils with high base saturation of the topsoil and low topsoil organic carbon. Also it seems to prefer agricultural  use areas, multi-lane road sides and areas near human settlements.

In another study,<ref>{{cite thesis|publisher=Aristotle University of Thessaloniki|title=Η επίδρασης της αλληλοπάθειας δασικών δέντρων στην εξάπλωση του είδους εισβολέα ''Solanum elaeagnifolium''|trans-title=Allelopathic effect of forest trees extracts on the distribution of the ''Solanum elaeagnifolium'' invasive species|url=http://ikee.lib.auth.gr/record/298909?ln=el |year=2018|lang=el}}</ref> on allelopathic effects with other plants, it was shown that white oak extract impedes its germination.

A five-year study found that frequent mowing of silverleaf nightshade contributes toward making it a 'superweed', with a deeper taproot, a spikier stem, and greater toxicity to grazing caterpillars.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Frequent mowing puts poisonous weed into survival mode |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2024/06/240603195751.htm |access-date=2024-06-04 |website=ScienceDaily |language=en}}</ref>
[[File:Solanum elaeagnifolium Paralia Macedonia Greece.jpg|thumb|Solanum elaeagnifolium in [[Paralia Katerinis|Paralia]],Greece.]]

==Toxicity==
The whole plant is toxic to both humans and livestock,<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.misin.msu.edu/facts/detail/?project=misin&id=404&cname=Silverleaf+nightshade | title=Factsheet, Silverleaf nightshade, Midwest Invasive Species Information Network (MISIN)}}</ref> even dried.<ref>https://poisonousplants.cvmbs.colostate.edu/plant/92</ref> 

Ingestion of silverleaf nightshade has been implicated as a cause of [[ivermectin]] toxicosis in horses given the recommended dosage of the drug.<ref>https://www.midriversequine.com/simultaneous-ivermectin-and-solanum-plant-poisoning-in-horses/</ref> Metabolites from the plant are speculated to disrupt the [[blood–brain barrier]], allowing ivermectin to enter and disrupt neurotransmitter function in the brain and spinal cord.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Swor|first1=TM|last2=Whittenburg|first2=JL|last3=Chaffin|first3=MK|title=Ivermectin toxicosis in three adult horses|journal=J Am Vet Med Assoc|date=2009|volume=235|issue=5|pages=558–62|doi=10.2460/javma.235.5.558|pmid=19719447|s2cid=8046553}}</ref>

Its thin spines can cause weed dermatitis.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.botanical-dermatology-database.info/BotDermFolder/SOLA.html | title=Acnistus, Atropa, Browallia, Brugmansia, Capsicum, Cestrum, Datura, Duboisia, Hyoscyamus, Lycium, Mandragora, Nicotiana, Petunia, Scopolia, Solandra, Solanum | SOLANACEAE: BoDD }}</ref>

The [[Pima people|Pima]] Native Americans used the berries as a vegetable [[rennet]], and the [[Kiowa]] used the seeds together with [[brain]] tissue to [[tanning (leather)|tan]] [[leather]].<ref name = wsnwcb2008 />

==Synonyms==
[[File:Solanum eleagnifolium az.jpg|thumb|right|Flowering branch of ''S. elaeagnifolium'']]
This plant has been described under a range of names, all now invalid. These contain many [[homonym]]s among them:<ref name = ss2008>Solanaceae Source [2008]</ref>
* ''Solanum dealbatum'' <small>Lindl.</small>
* ''Solanum flavidum'' <small>Torr.</small>
* ''Solanum incanum'' <small>Pav. ex Dunal (''non'' L.: [[Solanum incanum|preoccupied]])</small>
:''S. incanum'' of Ruiz & [[José Antonio Pavón Jiménez|Pavón Jiménez]] is ''[[Solanum albidum|S. albidum]]'' as described by [[Dunal]].	
:''S. incanum'' of [[Kitaibel]] based on Kanitz is ''[[Solanum villosum|S. villosum]]'' as described by [[Philip Miller]]
:''S. incanum'' of Scheff. is ''[[Solanum schefferi|S. schefferi]]''.
:''S. incanum'' var. ''lichtensteinii'' and var. ''subexarmatum'' are ''[[Solanum lichtensteinii|S. lichtensteinii]]''.
* ''Solanum leprosum'' <small>Ortega</small>
* ''Solanum obtusifolium'' <small>Dunal (''non'' Willd.: [[Solanum aethiopicum|preoccupied]])</small>
:''S. obtusifolium'' of [[Karl Theodor Hartweg|Hartweg]] based on [[Otto Sendtner]] in [[Carl Friedrich Philipp von Martius|von Martius]] is ''[[Solanum ferrugineum|S. ferrugineum]]''.
:''S. obtusifolium'' of [[Carl Ludwig Willdenow|Willdenow]] is ''[[Solanum aethiopicum|S. aethiopicum]]''.
* ''Solanum pyriforme var. uniflorum'' <small>Dunal</small>
* ''Solanum roemerianum'' <small>Scheele</small>
* ''Solanum saponaceum'' <small>Hook. (''non'' Dunal: [[Solanum saponaceum|preoccupied]])</small>
:''S. saponaceum'' of [[Friedrich Welwitsch|Welwitsch]] is ''[[Solanum aculeastrum|S. aculeastrum]]''.
:''S. saponaceum'' var. ''uruguense'' is ''[[Solanum bonariense|S. bonariense]]''.
* ''Solanum texense'' <small>Engelm. & A.Gray</small>
* ''Solanum uniflorum'' <small>Meyen ex Nees (''non'' Dunal: [[Lycianthes mociniana|preoccupied]])</small>
:''S. uniflorum'' of [[José Mariano de Conceição Vellozo|de Conceição Vellozo]] is ''[[Solanum pseudocapsicum|S. pseudocapsicum]]''. 	
:''S. uniflorum'' of Sessé & [[José Mariano Mociño|Mociño]] and ''S. uniflorum'' of Dunal in [[Jean Louis Marie Poiret|Poiret]] have been identified as ''[[Lycianthes mociniana]]''.
:''S. uniflorum'' of [[Mariano Lagasca y Segura|Lagasca y Segura]] and ''Solanum uniflorum var. berterianum'' are undetermined species of ''[[Lycianthes]]''.

Several [[variety (botany)|varieties]] and [[form (botany)|form]]s of ''S. elaeagnifolium'' have been named. They are not usually considered [[taxonomical]]ly distinct:<ref name = ss2008 />
* ''Solanum elaeagnifolium'' f. ''albiflorum'' <small>Cockerell</small>
* ''Solanum elaeagnifolium'' var. ''angustifolium'' <small>Kuntze</small>
:Not to be confused with ''[[Solanum angustifolium|S. angustifolium]]'' of Philip Miller
* ''Solanum elaeagnifolium'' var. ''argyrocroton'' <small>Griseb.</small>
* ''Solanum elaeagnifolium'' f. ''benkei'' <small>Standl.</small>
* ''Solanum elaeagnifolium'' var. ''grandiflorum'' <small>Griseb.</small>
:Not to be confused with ''[[Solanum grandiflorum|S. grandiflorum]]'' of Ruiz and Pavón Jiménez
* ''Solanum elaeagnifolium'' var. ''leprosum'' <small>(Ortega) Dunal</small>
* ''Solanum elaeagnifolium'' var. ''obtusifolium'' <small>(Dunal) Dunal</small>

''S. elaeagnifolium'' var. ''ovalifolium'' does not refer to the ''[[Solanum ovalifolium|S. ovalifolium]]'' as described by Dunal and does not belong to the present species; it is actually ''[[Solanum aridum|S. aridum]]''. Meanwhile, ''S. crispum'' var. ''elaeagnifolium'' is just the normal ''[[Solanum crispum|S. crispum]]'' of Ruiz and Pavón Jiménez.<ref name = ss2008 />
